title: Fewer and less, among and between, and other usage pairs
blurb: Choose fewer or less, number or amount, imply or infer, who or which, and other usage pairs by what the word must mean in the sentence.
question: A clinic report reads, “Fewer staff time was needed this month, and a large amount of patients implied from the new signs that the eminent change was good news.” Which words are used incorrectly, and what should replace them?

teach.h: Usage pairs: same family, different job
teach.body: Formally, a usage pair is two related words that standard English assigns to different meanings or grammatical jobs, such as fewer (countable nouns) and less (uncountable nouns). Plain English: both words are real and both look right, so spell-check and your ear will not save you. Decide what the blank must mean (a count? a speaker or a listener? a person or a thing?), then pick the word that carries that meaning.

teach.caption: Test: can you put a number in front of it (three tablets, three patients)? Then use fewer, number and many.

teach.body: Some plural-looking phrases are treated as single amounts, and “less” is standard with them: time (less than three weeks), money (less than $20), distance (less than 10 miles) and set phrases (25 words or less). The HESI A2 keys fewer only with clear count nouns such as patients, tablets, calories, complaints and staff members. “Less staff” is fine (staff as a group); “less staff members” is not.

teach.caption: The speaker puts the hint in (implies); the listener takes the meaning out (infers).
“The volunteer which greeted us” is an error (which is for things). “The nurse that helped me” is accepted in US usage, so it is not the tested error.

teach.body: The traditional guideline: between for two (between the two clinics), among for three or more (among the staff). Major US dictionaries also accept between for three or more items considered one by one (“a treaty between four nations”), so the HESI A2 does not make among or between the only error in a sentence. Learn the guideline, but look for a clearer error in the other options.

teach.h: Scenario: Noah fixes the clinic report
teach.body: Applicant Noah Kim, a front-desk worker, edits: “Fewer staff time was needed this month, and a large amount of patients implied from the new signs that the eminent change was good news.” Time is measured, so “less staff time.” Patients are counted, so “a large number of patients.” The patients drew the conclusion, so they “inferred.” A change about to happen is “imminent.” Four pairs, four fixes.

teach.text: The HESI A2 places the wrong twin where the sentence still sounds natural: “less complications,” “the amount of patients,” “the volunteer which,” “I implied from her tone.” Read for meaning: count or amount, speaker or listener, person or thing.

items: Fewer, number and many with countable nouns; less, amount and much with uncountable nouns.
Less is standard with time, money and distance (less than three weeks).
The speaker implies; the listener infers.
Who for people; which for things. That for people is accepted, so it is not keyed.
Among/between is a guideline only; eminent/imminent, elicit/illicit, personal/personnel, council/counsel, site/cite, weather/whether, all together/altogether are keyed by meaning.

summary: You can now choose fewer or less and number or amount by asking whether the noun can be counted, and pick imply or infer, who or which, and the other meaning pairs by what the sentence needs. You also know which pairs the HESI A2 treats only as preferences.

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The night shift has ___ nurses than the day shift.”
A.why: Nurses can be counted, so “fewer” is correct.

whyNot.0: “Less” is for uncountable amounts (less water), not countable nurses.
whyNot.2: “Lesser” means lower in importance or quality, not a smaller number.

options: The amount of visitors doubled during the holiday week.
The nurse recorded the amount of urine in the bag.
The number of paperwork on the desk kept growing.
A large amount of applicants missed the deadline.
A.why: Urine is measured, not counted, so “amount” is correct.

whyNot.0: Visitors can be counted, so the sentence needs “number.”
whyNot.2: Paperwork is uncountable, so the sentence needs “amount.”
whyNot.3: Applicants can be counted, so the sentence needs “number.”

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “From the doctor's careful wording, the family ___ that the news was serious.”
A.why: The family drew a conclusion from what they heard, so they “inferred.”

whyNot.0: “Implied” is what a speaker does (suggests); the family is the listener.
whyNot.2: “Insinuated” means hinted something unpleasant, which is also a speaker's act.
whyNot.3: “Intimated” means hinted, which is what a speaker does, not a listener.

B.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The nurse ___ answered the call light was new to the unit.”
B.why: “Who” refers to a person and is the subject of “answered.”

whyNot.2: “Whom” is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of “answered.”
whyNot.3: “Whose” shows possession and would need a noun after it.

B.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “The ___ surgeon said the storm's landfall was ___, so the team moved patients inland.”
B.why: “Eminent” means distinguished; “imminent” means about to happen.

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: a distinguished surgeon is “eminent,” and landfall about to happen is “imminent.”
whyNot.2: A landfall about to happen is “imminent.”

options: The new formula has less calories than the old one.
Patients reported fewer side effects on the new dose.
This month the clinic needed less interpreters.
The unit had less falls after the alarms were added.
B.why: Side effects can be counted, so “fewer side effects” is correct.

whyNot.0: Calories can be counted, so the sentence needs “fewer calories.”
whyNot.2: Interpreters can be counted, so the sentence needs “fewer interpreters.”
whyNot.3: Falls can be counted, so the sentence needs “fewer falls.”

C.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “Hospital ___ must lock their ___ phones in the staff lockers.”

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: staff are “personnel,” and one's own phone is “personal.”
whyNot.2: A phone that belongs to someone is “personal.”
whyNot.3: The staff of a hospital are its “personnel,” a noun.

C.q: Which sentence uses the commonly confused words correctly?
options: The counselor tried to illicit details about the fall.
The nurse cited the policy in her incident report.
The coordinator asked weather the drive was canceled.
The class waited altogether in the lobby for the tour.
C.why: “Cited” means referred to a source, which fits a policy named in a report.

whyNot.0: Drawing out details is “elicit”; “illicit” means illegal.
whyNot.3: Waiting as a group is “all together”; “altogether” means completely.

C.q: Which sentence avoids a usage error?
options: The city counsel voted to fund the new clinic.
Less than ten minutes passed before the ambulance arrived.
The amount of nurses on the floor was too low.
The patient implied from the sign that the clinic was closed.
C.why: Time is treated as a single amount, so “less than ten minutes” is standard.

whyNot.0: A governing group is a “council”; “counsel” means advice.
whyNot.2: Nurses can be counted, so the sentence needs “number.”
whyNot.3: The patient drew a conclusion, so the word is “inferred.”

reteach.title: Pills and syrup
reteach.question: At a pharmacy counter, some medicines come as pills you count and some as syrup you measure. How does that help you choose between fewer and less, number and amount?

blocks.h: Count the pills, measure the syrup
blocks.body: Pills are counted one by one: you take fewer pills, and the pharmacist checks the number of pills. Syrup is measured: you take less syrup, and the label states the amount of syrup. Any noun works the same way. Patients, calories and complaints behave like pills; water, pain and paperwork behave like syrup. Decide which it is before you choose the word.

blocks.text: Time and money are measured like syrup even when written with numbers: “less than an hour,” “less than $50.”

explain.body: Fewer goes with nouns you can count (fewer tablets); less goes with nouns you measure (less water). Time, money and distance usually take less.

test.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “Since the new policy, the unit has had ___ medication errors and ___ overtime.”
test.why: Errors can be counted (fewer errors); overtime is measured (less overtime).

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: countable errors take “fewer,” and uncountable overtime takes “less.”
whyNot.2: Errors can be counted, so they take “fewer.”
whyNot.3: Overtime is an amount, so it takes “less.”

explain.body: Number goes with countable plurals (the number of visits); amount goes with uncountable nouns (the amount of fluid).

test.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “The ___ of blood lost was small, but the ___ of stitches needed was high.”
test.why: Blood is measured (amount); stitches are counted (number).

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: blood is an amount, and stitches are a number.
whyNot.2: Stitches can be counted, so they take “number.”
whyNot.3: Blood is uncountable, so it takes “amount.”

explain.body: The speaker or writer implies (suggests without stating). The listener or reader infers (draws a conclusion).

options: The nurse inferred that the results were good by smiling.
From the empty lot, Ana implied that the clinic had closed.
The surgeon's pause implied that the news was not good.
The patient inferred to the staff that he was in pain.
test.why: The pause suggested the meaning without stating it, so it “implied” the news was not good.

whyNot.0: The nurse was signaling by smiling, so she “implied” it.
whyNot.1: Ana drew a conclusion from what she saw, so she “inferred.”
whyNot.3: Signaling something to others is “implying”; “inferred to” is not standard.

explain.body: Who refers to people; which refers to things and animals. That can refer to either and is accepted for people in US usage, so it is not the tested error.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The pharmacist ___ filled the order called to confirm the dose.”
test.why: “Who” refers to a person and is the subject of “filled.”

whyNot.0: “Which” refers to things, not to a pharmacist.
whyNot.2: “Whose” shows possession and would need a noun after it.
whyNot.3: “Whom” is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of “filled.”
